the path from $\vect{\mu}_\phi$ and $\vect{\sigma}_\phi$ to $\vect{z}$ is now

The move does not need a Gaussian. [Kingma and Welling](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114)
state it for any draw that can be written as

$$
\vect{z}=g_\phi(\vect{x},\vect{\epsilon}),
\qquad \vect{\epsilon}\sim r,
$$

where the base distribution $r$ does not depend on the learned parameters and $g_\phi$
is differentiable in them. Any location–scale family with a fixed standardized base
qualifies, since each of its draws is a shift and a scale of one base draw. What does
not carry over is the closed form in @eq-vae-diagonal-kl: another family needs its own
KL, or a Monte Carlo estimate of it.

edits.new:
For fixed generator density $p_g$ and an unrestricted discriminator, the maximizer can
be found point by point. When $\vect{z}\sim p_z$, the sample
$\vect{x}=G_\theta(\vect{z})$ has density $p_g$, so the second expectation in $V$ is an
expectation over $\vect{x}\sim p_g$:

$$
V(D,G)
=\int\Big[p_{\mathrm{data}}(\vect{x})\log D(\vect{x})
+p_g(\vect{x})\log\big(1-D(\vect{x})\big)\Big]\,d\vect{x}.
$$

At each $\vect{x}$, write $a=p_{\mathrm{data}}(\vect{x})$, $b=p_g(\vect{x})$, and
$u=D(\vect{x})$. For positive $a$ and $b$, the integrand $a\log u+b\log(1-u)$ is concave
in $u\in(0,1)$, so its maximum is the stationary point where

$$
\frac{a}{u}-\frac{b}{1-u}=0,
$$

namely

$$
D^*(\vect{x})
edits.note: Pointwise argument: the second expectation over x ~ p_g, concavity in u, the stationary point. New material (W9 exposition brief); outside the voice passes under N1.

edits.old:
Substituting $D^*$ into the value gives

$$
V(D^*,G)
=-\log 4
+2D_{\mathrm{JS}}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\,\|\,p_g),
$$ {#eq-gan-js}

where $D_{\mathrm{JS}}$ is Jensen--Shannon divergence. The ideal function-space
minimum occurs at $p_g=p_{\mathrm{data}}$, where $D^*=1/2$, an observed neural
discriminator near one half does not certify that equilibrium; it may also be weak,
undertrained, or locally confused.
edits.new:
Substituting $D^*$ into $V$, with the mixture
$m=\tfrac12(p_{\mathrm{data}}+p_g)$, so that $D^*=p_{\mathrm{data}}/(2m)$ and
$1-D^*=p_g/(2m)$, splits a $-\log 2$ off each logarithm; each density integrates to
one, so

$$
V(D^*,G)
=-\log 4
+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\,\|\,m)
+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_g\,\|\,m).
$$

The Jensen--Shannon divergence is the average of those two KL terms,
$D_{\mathrm{JS}}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\,\|\,p_g)
=\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\,\|\,m)
+\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_g\,\|\,m)$, so their sum is twice it:

$$
V(D^*,G)
=-\log 4
+2D_{\mathrm{JS}}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\,\|\,p_g).
$$ {#eq-gan-js}

The ideal function-space minimum occurs at $p_g=p_{\mathrm{data}}$, where $D^*=1/2$.
An observed neural discriminator near one half does not certify that equilibrium; it
may also be weak, undertrained, or locally confused.
edits.note: Introduces m, shows the intermediate KL equality, defines JSD before the identity; fixes the comma splice after D* = 1/2. New material (W9 exposition brief); outside the voice passes under N1.
